abstract: In the post-extinction period, does evolutionary capacity recover together with biomass? We address this question with a consumer resource model in which strategies lie on a rate-yield (opportunist gleaner) trade-off and dissipate the substrate free energy they do not conserve in biomass. We track biomass-specific dissipation, s, a model-based proxy for specific entropy production. After a reset, abundant resources favor fast, low-yield strategies, and s is high; this rate selection resembles, but does not demonstrate, the maximum power principle. As resources are drawn down, competitive exclusion favors high-yield strategies and lowers s, provided that turnover is low and that affinity is lost faster than growth rate is gained along the trade-off. In finite populations, the high-dissipation phase returned after a reset only if a reservoir of costly strategies, here dormant propagules, had persisted since those strategies were last abundant; its return fell from 199 to 33 of 200 runs as the reservoir decayed. Biomass recovered in every run, and sooner when the high-dissipation phase failed to return. Ecological recovery and recovery of evolutionary capacity are therefore distinct. We state falsifiable predictions for calorimetric chemostat experiments with graded bottlenecks and controlled resting-stage survival.
